reason: The stream's top match in the chapter at rarity 2.00, and it scores on five words of connective tissue that the Book of Mormon uses continuously. 2 Kings 17:14 is about Israel hardening their necks like their fathers; Helaman 16:2 and 16:6 are about a crowd that did not believe in the words of Samuel. Nothing but the negated verb and its preposition is shared, and 'believe in' is among the commonest constructions in either book. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; recorded here only because it outranked every real link in the chapter.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'cast stones at' occurs only at 2 Samuel 16:6, where Shimei stones David and his servants as the king flees Absalom — and tempting for exactly that reason. It is the wrong story. Shimei's stones are an insult thrown at a fleeing king by a partisan of the house he displaced, and they land; the stones at Helaman 16:2 are thrown by a whole city at a prophet standing still on a wall, and they miss, which is the point of the verse. The KJV passage that is doing the work here is Matthew 23:37, the city that stones the prophets sent to it, which Samuel had already put to this same city at Helaman 13:25; the link is filed there. The singleton is a coincidence of a common verb and a common noun, and is a good illustration of why a rarity count is evidence and not a verdict.

Five words shared and the senses are unrelated. In Jeremiah 8:7 the stork, the turtle, the crane and the swallow 'observe the time of their coming' — bird migration, cited as a reproach to a people who do not know the LORD's judgment. In Helaman 16:5 'the time of their coming' is the arrival of prophesied events, so that hearers may remember they were told beforehand. The pronoun does not even refer to persons in the same way: Jeremiah's 'their' is the birds', the Book of Mormon's is the things'. An artifact of English word order, and a clean example of the trap at ADJUDICATING §4.

'Cast himself down' is a KJV singleton and it is not this. At 1 Kings 18:42 Elijah goes up to the top of Carmel and casts himself down upon the earth, putting his face between his knees to pray for rain — a prostration, not a fall. Samuel casts himself down from the wall to escape a mob. Checked because the singleton would have made a strong-looking row; the link at this verse goes instead to Luke 4:9, whose 'cast thyself down from hence' is the right act and the right preposition even though it is second person. Recorded so that a reader who runs the rarity count themselves finds the Elijah verse already accounted for.

The stream's best match at this verse (rarity 2.00), and the resemblance is entirely in a narrative formula. Matthew 4:17 begins Jesus' Galilean ministry, 'From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent'; Helaman 16:7 ends Samuel's, sending him home to 'begin to preach and to prophesy among his own people'. The pairing in the Book of Mormon is preach-and-prophesy, not preach-and-say, and 'began to preach' carries no distinctive KJV colour. The chapter's real Matthew contact is at 16:6.

A batch entry covering the chapter's regnal formula, which the stream matches at 16:9 (Ezra 6:15, 1 Kings 16:8, 2 Chronicles 36:20), 16:11, 16:12 and 16:24. 'The eighty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges' is the Book of Mormon's own dating formula, used through Alma and Helaman without variation, and it happens to share its skeleton with every regnal date in Kings, Chronicles and Ezra because both are King James English for the same thing. The rare words the scorer rewards — 'reign', 'sixth' — are supplied by the calendar, not by a source. No entry in this family is a borrowing.

sharedText: their own strength ... their own wisdom
reason: 'Began to depend upon their own strength, and upon their own wisdom' reads like wisdom literature and is not traceable to any of it. 'Own strength' occurs in two KJV verses (Psalm 21:13, Amos 6:13) and 'own wisdom' in one (Proverbs 23:4, 'cease from thine own wisdom'), and none of them pairs the two or supplies the verb. Proverbs 3:5's 'lean not unto thine own understanding' is the sentiment but not the noun, and Isaiah 5:21's 'wise in their own eyes' is neither. A real conceptual resemblance with too little verbal contact to adjudicate. The chapter's argument about wisdom and folly is carried instead by the Ephesians 5:15 link at 16:10.

Worth recording because of what it shows about the Book of Mormon's English rather than about a source. 'The evil one' is not a King James phrase: the KJV's designation is 'the wicked one' (Matthew 13:19, 13:38, 1 John 2:13, 2:14), and the only string match for 'evil one' in the whole King James Bible is the word-boundary artifact at James 4:11, 'Speak not evil one of another'. So Helaman 16:21's 'the cunning and the mysterious arts of the evil one' is a place where the text is not following the KJV even where a KJV equivalent was available. No link; the observation belongs in the register.

The stream's only match at this verse, on 'them all the days of'. Isaiah 63:9 is the angel of God's presence bearing and carrying Israel all the days of old; Helaman 16:21 is a fear of being kept in servitude 'all the days of our lives'. The shared string is a time adverbial that occurs across the KJV in every genre and completes differently in the two verses — 'of old' against 'of our lives'. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A batch entry for the connective matches at 16:22 and 16:23. 'Upon all the face of the land' is a Book of Mormon geographical formula used scores of times from 1 Nephi onward and adjudicated at its first use; the machine matches it here against Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock, and matches the same two verses against Exodus 14:17 and Joshua 7:5 on 'harden the hearts of' and 'hearts of the people', against 2 Chronicles 14:2 and 31:20 on 'that which was good and', against Luke 1:66 on 'up in their hearts', and against Deuteronomy 1:36 on 'the land that he'. None shares a content word that construes with its match. The real source at 16:22 is Psalm 2:1, which the stream did not propose, because the agreement is split across the sentence and contiguous windows cannot see it (CONVENTIONS §9).

The stream's highest-scoring candidate at this verse (rarity 2.00, a six-word run) and the wrong one. Deuteronomy 34:11 shares the formula 'the signs and the wonders' with Helaman 16:23, and so, on the stream's own list, do Deuteronomy 7:19 and twelve other KJV verses; the phrase identifies nothing. What identifies the source is the clause the stream ranked last, at rarity 1.00: 'wrought among the people' is a KJV singleton at Acts 5:12, which is also the only verse in the Bible carrying the whole of 'signs and wonders wrought among the people'. Deuteronomy's signs are Moses' plagues on Pharaoh; Helaman's are worked among the Lord's own people and fail to hold them, which is Acts 5:12's situation inverted. The link is filed at this verse to Acts 5:12.
